name: Eventward
author: OmnisWP

sections.description:
Eventward is a complete events calendar for WordPress, and all of it is free. Recurring events, six calendar views, maps, venues, organizers, tickets and RSVP come in one plugin. There is no Pro version, no add-on store, no licence key and no feature held back for a paid tier.

It is built for sites that need to stay fast and correct: event dates live in their own indexed table, repeating schedules are expanded by a real iCalendar engine, and paid tickets go straight to your own Stripe account with no fee from us.

What makes Eventward different

  • Everything is in the free plugin. Recurring events, every view, maps, filters, tickets and RSVP. Most event plugins sell these as add-ons; here there is nothing to upgrade to.
  • Built on a proper date index. Each event date is stored as a row in one small indexed table, instead of being searched out of post meta. Month, week and list views stay quick as a calendar grows into thousands of dates, and every event keeps its real post ID, so other plugins and page builder loops work with it normally.
  • Recurring events that get the details right. Schedules follow the iCalendar standard (RRULE), with skipped and extra dates. Each event has its own timezone, and a 7pm weekly event stays at 7pm when the clocks change.
  • Tickets with no platform fee. Free tickets work as an RSVP. Paid tickets use Stripe Checkout on your own Stripe account: buyers pay you directly and you only pay Stripe’s standard processing fees.
  • Search engine friendly by design. Every event page carries schema.org Event data for Google. Calendar navigation cannot turn into an endless crawl: dated calendar pages are noindex, navigation links are nofollow and empty far-future months return 404.
  • An easy move from The Events Calendar. A built-in importer copies your events, venues, organizers, categories, ticket types and bookings across without changing anything in The Events Calendar. Event, venue, organizer, month and day URLs follow the same patterns, and an optional setting lets existing [tribe_events] shortcodes keep working, so links and pages survive the switch.
  • Bring your events from anywhere else too. Import from All-in-One Event Calendar, from Eventbrite, from calendar files (.ics) exported by Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar, or from a spreadsheet. Calendar feeds can keep syncing on a schedule.

Calendar and views

  • Six views: month, week, list, photo, map and day, as a block you can place anywhere, plus ready-made templates for block themes. Classic themes are supported too.
  • Search and filters by keyword, category, venue and organizer, applied in place without reloading the page.
  • Mobile friendly. On small screens the month view becomes an easy-to-read agenda.
  • Category colours. Give each category a colour and show it as a line before each event or as the event’s background in the month and week views.
  • Your choice of display. 24-hour or 12-hour times, and full event names in the month view for long titles.
  • Light on your pages. Styles and scripts only load where events are shown, and moving between months and views updates the calendar in place.

Recurring events and time zones

  • Daily, weekly, monthly (“the second Tuesday”, “the last Friday”) and yearly schedules, with intervals, end dates, counts, skipped dates and extra dates (each at the usual time or its own).
  • A custom option for anything else the iCalendar standard can describe.
  • A timezone per event, with correct local times across daylight saving changes.
  • Each date of a repeating event has its own page and its own entry in Google’s event data.

Venues, organizers and maps

  • Create venues and organizers inline while editing an event. Each gets its own page listing its upcoming events.
  • Maps without API keys. OpenStreetMap maps for the calendar, venues and events, with clustered pins, bundled with the plugin.
  • Place venues by typing their coordinates, or turn on address lookup (OpenStreetMap Nominatim, off by default) to find them from the address when you save.

Tickets and RSVP

  • Free RSVP and paid tickets, several ticket types per event, with capacity per type and per date.
  • Stripe Checkout in test and live mode. Connect your Stripe account in one click, or paste a restricted API key.
  • Seats are held while a buyer pays and released automatically if they do not finish, so a date does not oversell.
  • Confirmation emails with ticket codes, an attendee list with check-in, CSV export, one-click refunds and resending confirmations.
  • Your own booking questions on each ticket type (short or long text, dropdown, yes-or-no tick box, phone number), answered once per ticket, with answers on the attendee list, in the CSV and in the emails. Logged-in visitors find their name and email already filled in, which suits membership sites.
  • Reports: bookings, check-ins, no-shows and takings by month, by date and by ticket type for any period, with capacity filled per date and a CSV export for your annual figures.
  • An optional Stripe webhook for instant confirmations. Without it, payments are still confirmed when buyers return and by a background check.
  • Bookings are included in WordPress’s personal data export and erasure tools.

Events sent in by your community

  • A form for your site where people suggest events without a login to wp-admin: name, date and times, description, category, cost, website and an image, a venue and organizer picked from your own lists (or typed in), and their name and email.
  • Every event sent waits as Pending, like a comment awaiting moderation. You are emailed, the Events menu shows how many are waiting, and nothing is public until you publish it. The sender can be emailed when it goes live.
  • Add it with the Submit Event Form block or the [eventward_submit] shortcode. Choose who may send events (anyone, or logged-in people only) under Events > Settings.

Themes, blocks and page builders

  • Native blocks and Site Editor templates for block themes.
  • Shortcodes for the calendar, event details, single fields (date, venue, cost and more), tickets, maps and the event submission form, for Bricks, Divi, Elementor and other builders.
  • A sortable “next date” field for page builder query loops.

Sharing and SEO

  • schema.org Event data on every event: status, attendance mode, location, organizer, price and availability.
  • Add to calendar links for Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, Outlook and Microsoft 365, plus subscribable iCal feeds for the whole calendar or any category.
  • Event status for cancelled, postponed, rescheduled and moved online events, shown on the page and sent to Google.

Fair by default

  • No upsells, no admin banners, no ads and no tracking. Every external service Eventward can use is listed below, with what it sends and when.
  • Your data stays yours: deactivating never deletes anything, and uninstalling only removes events if you ask it to.
  • Translation ready.

Eventward is made by OmnisWP, the team behind Siteward.

External services

Eventward works on your own site, except for the services below:

  • OpenStreetMap Nominatim (geocoding). Off by default: nothing is sent until an admin turns on address lookup under Events > Settings > Maps. When on, it turns venue addresses into map locations. Your site contacts https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org when a venue is saved with a new or changed address, when you press “Find on map”, and in an hourly background check that looks up to 10 venues that have never been looked up (for example imported ones). Venues whose coordinates you typed yourself are never looked up. Each request sends the venue’s address (street, city, region, postcode, country), your site’s address (in the User-Agent, as Nominatim’s policy requires) and your site’s language. Nothing about your visitors is sent. You can turn it off again at any time. Usage policy: https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/nominatim/ Privacy policy: https://osmfoundation.org/wiki/Privacy_Policy
  • OpenStreetMap map tiles. Pages that show a map load map images from https://tile.openstreetmap.org in the visitor’s browser (only once the map scrolls into view). The visitor’s IP address and the page address are visible to that server, as with any image. Tile usage policy: https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/tiles/ Privacy policy: https://osmfoundation.org/wiki/Privacy_Policy You can switch to another tile provider under Events > Settings > Maps.
  • Add to calendar links (Google Calendar, Outlook.com, Microsoft 365) are ordinary links: nothing is sent unless a visitor clicks one.
  • Stripe (payments). Only when you sell paid tickets. Your site talks to https://api.stripe.com to create Stripe Checkout sessions, confirm payments and make refunds. For each checkout your site sends the buyer’s email address, the event title, date and time, the tickets with their prices, an order reference and the addresses of your event page that Stripe returns the buyer to; card details are entered on Stripe’s own page and never touch your site. If you add the optional webhook in your Stripe Dashboard, Stripe also sends payment and refund notices to your site. Stripe terms: https://stripe.com/legal Privacy policy: https://stripe.com/privacy
  • OmnisWP connection service. Only if you choose “Connect with Stripe” instead of pasting an API key. Stripe’s app login needs a secret held by OmnisWP, so https://omniswp.com/wp-json/omnis-connect/v1 is contacted only when an admin presses “Connect with Stripe” (your site first checks the service is available for that mode), and while connected, to renew the short-lived access token: by a background check every 30 minutes, and on demand if the token has run out when your site next talks to Stripe (for example during a booking). When connecting, the admin’s browser takes the mode (test or live), a one-time challenge and the address of your site’s Payments screen to omniswp.com, and your site then sends the one-time claim code and its matching secret to collect the tokens. When renewing, your site sends the mode and the refresh token. Like any WordPress request, these carry your site’s address in the User-Agent. The service never sees payments or buyer details, and keeps nothing after handing the tokens to your site. Terms: https://omniswp.com/terms/ Privacy policy: https://omniswp.com/privacy-policy/
  • Calendar feeds (import, optional). Off until an admin adds a feed under Events > Import > Calendar file or feed. Your site then fetches that address from its own server: once to check it, then on the schedule chosen (hourly, twice a day or daily), and whenever an admin presses Sync now or imports an address with WP-CLI. The requests go only to the addresses you entered (for example Google Calendar or Outlook), identify themselves as Eventward without your site’s address, and carry nothing about your visitors. Delete the feed to stop them. The terms and privacy policy of the calendar service you use apply.
  • Eventbrite (import, optional). Nothing is sent until an admin pastes a private token under Events > Import > Eventbrite and presses Connect. Your site then contacts https://www.eventbriteapi.com to check the token and list the account’s organizations, to count the chosen organization’s events while the Import screen is open, and during an import to read the events, their descriptions, venues, organizers and ticket types. Each request sends the token (in a header), which organization and events to read and, like any WordPress request, your site’s address in the User-Agent. Nothing on Eventbrite is changed and nothing about your visitors is sent. The token is stored encrypted on your site, with the account’s name, email address and organization names, until you press Forget token. Terms: https://www.eventbrite.com/corporate/legal/legalterms/ API terms: https://www.eventbrite.com/help/en-us/articles/833731/eventbrite-api-terms-of-use/ Privacy policy: https://www.eventbrite.com/help/en-us/articles/460838/eventbrite-privacy-policy/
  • Event images during an import. When an import from a calendar file, feed, spreadsheet or Eventbrite includes image addresses and downloading images is ticked (it is by default), your site downloads each image once from the address given (for example Eventbrite’s image server, img.evbuc.com) and adds it to your media library. For feeds this also happens during the scheduled sync. Like any WordPress request, these carry your site’s address in the User-Agent.

Third-party libraries

  • Leaflet 1.9.4, BSD 2-Clause licence, https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet (bundled in assets/vendor/leaflet, minified build from the official npm package)
  • Leaflet.markercluster 1.5.3, MIT licence, https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet.markercluster (bundled in assets/vendor/leaflet-markercluster)
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate Eventward from Plugins > Add New.
  2. Go to Events > Add Event. Set the date, time and repeat options in the Event settings box under the content, and add a venue and organizer if you like.
  3. Your calendar is live at /events/. To show it anywhere else, add the Events Calendar block, or the [eventward] shortcode in a page builder.
  4. To take bookings, turn on “Take bookings for this event” in the Tickets and RSVP panel. Free tickets work straight away; for paid tickets, connect Stripe under Events > Payments.
  5. Adjust views, slugs, maps and more under Events > Settings.
sections.faq:
Is there a Pro version?

No. Every feature is in this plugin, free.

Will it slow my site down?

Eventward only loads its styles and scripts on pages that show events, and stores event dates in an indexed table built for date-range lookups.

Do you take a fee on ticket sales?

No. Payments go directly from the buyer to your own Stripe account. You only pay Stripe’s standard processing fees.

Do I need a Stripe account?

Only for paid tickets. Free tickets (RSVP) work without Stripe or any other service.

I use The Events Calendar. Can I bring my events across?

Yes. Go to Events > Import (or run wp eventward import-tec). It copies your events, venues, organizers, categories, tags, featured images and ticket types (with their sale dates, and Event Tickets Plus attendee fields as booking questions), and other custom fields such as SEO titles and descriptions. Repeating events from Events Calendar Pro come across as repeat rules where Eventward can read them, otherwise as their list of dates. Bookings come across too: paid orders (Tickets Commerce, PayPal and WooCommerce), RSVPs and their attendees, with check-ins, answers and ticket codes. Unpaid orders and “not going” RSVPs are left out. Nothing is charged, refunded or emailed, and nothing in The Events Calendar is changed, so you can check first, run it again later, and keep The Events Calendar until you are happy.

Can I import from another calendar, Eventbrite or a spreadsheet?

Yes, all under Events > Import. Each import can be checked first without changing anything (calendar feeds simply sync), and what it brought in can be moved to the trash again:

  • All-in-One Event Calendar: events, categories with their colours, and the venues and contacts typed into each event. Works with that plugin inactive, and wp eventward import-ai1ec runs it from the command line, once per site on a network.
  • Calendar files (.ics) exported by Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple Calendar and others, with repeat rules, changed and cancelled dates and time zones. Add a calendar’s .ics address as a feed instead and Eventward keeps it in step every hour, twice a day or daily.
  • Spreadsheets (.csv): match each column to an event field, with a preview. Exports from The Events Calendar, Google Calendar and Outlook are recognised. Ids from a spreadsheet only match events from the same spreadsheet, so two files that both number their rows never overwrite each other; name a spreadsheet to keep matching it after renaming its columns. A sample file is on the screen.
  • Eventbrite (beta): paste a private token from your Eventbrite account. Ticket types can come across, with bookings turned off: selling the same event in both places would oversell. Orders and attendees stay on Eventbrite.

I use The Events Calendar. Will my links break if I switch?

Eventward uses the same URL patterns for events, venues, organizers and calendar pages, and the importer keeps each event’s address, so existing links keep working. If your pages use the [tribe_events] shortcode, turn on its compatibility option under Events > Settings once The Events Calendar is deactivated.

Eventward is an independent plugin by OmnisWP. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by The Events Calendar, All-in-One Event Calendar, Eventbrite or the other products named here, or their makers; their names are used only to describe compatibility.

I use the Classic Editor (or Divi). Where are the event fields?

On the classic edit screen they are in boxes below the content: Date and time (including repeats), Event details and Tickets and RSVP. Venues and organizers have their own boxes too. With the block editor they are in the Event settings box under the content (or in the sidebar, if you choose that from the Options menu).

Can visitors send in their own events?

Yes. Add the Submit Event Form block (or the [eventward_submit] shortcode) to a page. Events sent with it are saved as Pending with the sender’s name and email; you get an email with a link to review it, and the Events menu shows a count like Comments. Open the event, make any changes, and publish it. A venue or organizer the sender typed in is published with it, and the sender is emailed once that the event is live. Under Events > Settings > Event submissions you choose who may send events, where the emails go, and whether new venues, organizers and images are allowed. The form has spam protection built in (a hidden trap field, a minimum time to fill it in and a limit per connection), and works without JavaScript.

Does it work with my theme or page builder?

Yes. Block themes get native blocks and templates, classic themes are supported, and shortcodes cover Bricks, Divi, Elementor and other builders.

Can I translate the calendar with TranslatePress, WPML or Polylang?

Yes. Every word Eventward shows comes from its translation file (apart from text you type into its settings, such as the description heading), so the simplest route is a language pack: translations made on translate.wordpress.org arrive with updates automatically. The data-no-translation attribute you may see on calendar labels is added by TranslatePress itself, to mark text that comes from a plugin.

Does Eventward contact any outside services?

Only the ones listed under External services below, each for a clear reason: map tiles when a map is shown, venue address lookups only if you turn them on, Stripe when you sell paid tickets, the OmnisWP connection service only if you use one-click Stripe connection, and the calendar feeds, Eventbrite account or image addresses you choose to import from. There is no tracking or usage reporting, and nothing is sent until you use the feature concerned.

Which recurrence rules are supported?

Daily, weekly, monthly and yearly rules with intervals, weekdays, “nth weekday” and “last weekday” patterns, end dates and counts. The custom option accepts iCalendar RRULEs using FREQ, INTERVAL, COUNT, UNTIL, BYDAY, BYMONTHDAY, BYMONTH, BYSETPOS and WKST.
sections.changelog:
0.7.4

  • Fix: A calendar file where one week of a series is moved to another time (the date skipped and added again at the new time, which is how Eventward’s own feeds write it) now imports with that week at its new time. Before, the moved date was lost, from .ics files and feeds and from The Events Calendar Pro. The calendar file also leaves out an extra date on a day the editor skips, as the site does.
  • Change: Importing a calendar file warns when an extra date falls on a day the series already has at another time, since Eventward keeps one time a day.
  • Fix: Deleting a submitted event for good keeps its image when another post uses it, such as a copy made with Duplicate.
  • Fix: Saving a Settings page that was left open from before an update no longer turns the tickets and event submission switches off.
  • Fix: The Submit Event Form and booking form keep their hidden spam trap hidden even when a speed plugin delays or removes the stylesheet.
  • Fix: Submit Event Form: the thank-you message is announced to screen readers, an error marks the right field (the end date, or the end time), and the hint under the email and image fields is still read out next to an error.
  • Fix: Submit Event Form: tighter limits against scripts (an animated GIF counts every frame towards the picture size limit, a very busy server refuses a send rather than skipping the hourly limit, and fewer stored refills per connection).
  • Fix: Export and Erase Personal Data also find events sent while logged in, and include the account and image.
  • Fix: On the classic edit screen, clearing the start date for a moment no longer stops the end date following it.

0.7.3

  • New: “Show repeating events once” for the Events Calendar block in list, photo and map views (or [eventward repeats="once"]). A course of four weekly sessions shows as one entry at its next date, with how many dates it has (“4 dates, 3 Dec to 24 Dec 2026”); the event page still lists every date. Turn on “Hide a course once it has started” (or started="hide") to leave out courses whose first date has begun, for courses people book as a whole; repeats with no end date still show at their next date. Asked for by a sewing school whose visitors took each session for a new course.
  • New: “Number the dates of a series” for the same block (or numbers="yes") shows “Session 2 of 4” on each date of a repeating event that has an end.
  • New: Events > Settings > Calendar: choose the separator between an event’s time, place and cost in lists (· by default, or | or / and so on).
  • New: Events > Settings > Calendar: a heading for the event description. When set, event pages put the description in its own section (class ew-description) under that heading, for styling. Off unless you give it a heading.
  • Change: The separator between an event’s time, place and cost keeps a small gap on themes that lay that line out differently.
  • Change: In the editor (block and classic), the end date and “Last date” pickers open at the start date and offer nothing earlier. On the classic edit screen, moving the start date now moves the end date by the same number of days, keeping the event’s length as the block editor does.

0.7.2

  • Fix: The Submit Event Form refused times that were not on a 5-minute step (9:21, for example). Any minute is accepted now.
  • Fix: Website and link fields on the Submit Event Form accept addresses typed without https:// (www.example.com.au), as the form already handled them, instead of the browser asking for a full URL.
  • Fix: Previewing a draft or pending event (for example one sent in through the form) now shows its dates, venue, map and organizer as the published page will, instead of an empty details panel. Only people who can edit the event see this.
  • Change: Links to other sites on event, venue and organizer pages (event website, join online, organizer and venue websites, View map, Google and Outlook calendar links) open in a new tab, so visitors keep your site open. Screen readers are told the link opens a new tab.

0.7.1

  • New: Extra dates can start at their own time. In the Repeats card, pick a time beside each date you add (for example a play on Friday at 7:30 pm and Saturday at 3 pm); the event keeps the same length on every date. On the classic edit screen, write the time after the date (2026-11-21 15:00). An extra date on a day the repeat rule already covers replaces that day’s time. Calendar files (.ics) and Google Calendar links carry each date’s own time.
  • New: Events > Settings > Tickets and RSVP turns bookings off for the whole site. Sites that only list events no longer see the Tickets card in the editor, the Attendees, Reports and Payments screens, the Tickets column or any booking form. Nothing is deleted: ticket types and bookings come back when you turn it on again, and links in booking emails keep working (also when bookings are turned off for one event).
  • Change: Importing from The Events Calendar, calendar files (.ics) and feeds keeps the start time of dates that start at a different time from the first, instead of moving them to the first date’s time.

0.7.0

  • New: Event submissions. A form for your site where people suggest events without a login to wp-admin: event name, date and times (or all day), description, categories, cost, website and an image; a venue and organizer chosen from your lists, typed in (“Somewhere else”, “Someone else”) or online with a link to join; and their own name and email. Add it with the Submit Event Form block or [eventward_submit].
  • New: Each event sent is saved as Pending, with any venue or organizer typed in. You get an email with the details and a “Review and publish” button (reply to it to write to the sender), the Events menu shows how many are waiting, and the Events list marks each one “Sent by”. Publishing the event publishes its new venue and organizer too, and emails the sender once that it is live.
  • New: Events > Settings > Event submissions: anyone or only logged-in people, where the emails go, and whether visitors may add new venues and organizers, upload an image, and be emailed when their event is published.
  • New: The form checks every field on the server and comes back filled in after a mistake. Spam protection: a hidden trap field, a minimum time to fill it in, a limit of 5 events an hour per connection (not for editors), and a key per form so a double tap sends one event. Images are checked to be real JPG, PNG, WebP or GIF files up to 5 MB.
  • New: Senders’ names and emails are included in Tools > Export Personal Data and Erase Personal Data, and the suggested privacy policy text covers them.

0.6.0

  • New: Events > Import now has a tab for each source, and four new importers. Each has a check first that changes nothing, can refresh events imported before, and can move everything it imported to the trash.
  • New: Import from All-in-One Event Calendar (Timely), or run wp eventward import-ai1ec (once per site on a network). Copies events with their dates, repeat rules and time zones, categories with their colours, tags and featured images, and turns the venues and contacts typed into each event into shared venues and organizers. Repeat rules come across when Eventward reads them the same way, otherwise the generated dates are copied. Events it pulled in from calendar feeds are left out unless you ask for them. Works with All-in-One Event Calendar inactive and never changes its data.
  • New: Import calendar files (.ics) from Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple Calendar, Meetup, The Events Calendar and others, with repeat rules, changed and cancelled dates, time zones (including Outlook’s Windows names), venues, organizers, categories and images.
  • New: Calendar feeds. Add a calendar’s .ics address and Eventward keeps its events in step every hour, twice a day or daily: new events are added, changed ones updated, and future events removed from the feed go to the trash. Events you trash or delete yourself stay out. A reply that stops before the end of the calendar is ignored, and a feed that suddenly has no events, or less than half of what it had, keeps its events and shows a warning instead. Only one sync of a feed runs at a time. Repeating events whose start is in UTC stay in UTC, so their dates match the calendar after daylight saving changes. wp eventward feeds manages them from the command line.
  • New: Import events from a spreadsheet (.csv), or run wp eventward import-csv. Match each column to an event field with a preview of the first rows; exports from The Events Calendar, Google Calendar and Outlook are matched automatically. Reads CSV files saved from Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers in any common encoding or separator and dates in most formats, working out day-first or month-first dates from the whole file. A sample file is on the screen.
  • New (beta): Import your Eventbrite events with a private token from your Eventbrite account, or run wp eventward import-eventbrite: titles, descriptions, dates in each event’s time zone, venues, organizers, categories and images. A series becomes one event with extra dates when every date shares its time. Ticket types can come across too, with bookings turned off so nothing is sold twice; refreshing never changes the ticket types of an event whose bookings you turned on here. Eventbrite is only contacted after you connect (see External services).
  • New: Ticket sale dates. Each ticket type can have “On sale from” and “On sale until” (in the event’s time zone). The booking form shows when sales open or that they have ended (with the event’s time zone when it differs from the site’s), and bookings outside those dates are refused. A date picked without a time runs from the start of the first day to the end of the last.
  • New: The importer for The Events Calendar now brings bookings across: paid orders from Tickets Commerce, PayPal and WooCommerce, RSVPs and their attendees, with check-ins, answers to attendee questions and ticket codes. Nothing is charged, refunded or emailed. Imported bookings count toward capacity, show in Attendees (marked “Imported”) and in Reports, and can be cancelled to free the seat (refunds are made where they were paid). Refreshing keeps each check-in and ticket code with the same person, and keeps bookings you cancelled in Eventward cancelled unless The Events Calendar changed them since. Turn it off with “Import bookings” or --no-bookings.
  • Change: Ticket sale dates from The Events Calendar come across, so tickets whose sales ended are kept, marked “Sales ended”, instead of being left out.
  • Change: The Import screen says more clearly that events, ticket types and bookings come across from The Events Calendar, not only venues, organizers and categories.
  • Fix: wp eventward import-tec --no-tickets and --no-custom-fields were refused by WP-CLI.
  • Fix: Duplicating an imported event no longer copies its import marker, so moving imported items to the trash never touches the copy.
  • Change: Moving an import’s items to the trash leaves venues and organizers that other events still use.
  • Change: The Classic Editor warns when ticket sales end before they start, and its tickets table scrolls on its own on small screens.
  • New: “+ New venue” and “+ New organizer” in the event now take every detail, not just the name: address, city, region, postcode, country, phone and website for a venue; email, phone and website for an organizer. With a venue chosen, “Edit venue details” opens it in a new tab. The Classic Editor has the same fields, and creates the venue or organizer when you save the event. People who may not publish venues or organizers (Contributors) add them as pending, for an editor to check. Thanks to Hans-Gerd Gerhards for the idea.
  • Fix: The “View map” link under a venue’s address searched OpenStreetMap for the venue’s name and address together, which often found nothing. It now searches for the address alone, leaving out units and floors (“Level 2”) that OpenStreetMap cannot find. Venues with map coordinates still link to their exact spot.

Earlier versions

The changes in 0.5.10 and earlier are in changelog.txt, in the plugin’s folder.

  • Recurring events that get the details right. Schedules follow the iCalendar standard (RRULE), with skipped and extra dates. Each event has its own timezone, and a 7pm weekly event stays at 7pm when the clocks change.
  • Tickets with no platform fee. Free tickets work as an RSVP. Paid tickets use Stripe Checkout on your own Stripe account: buyers pay you directly and you only pay Stripe’s standard processing fees.
  • Search engine friendly by design. Every event page carries schema.org Event data for Google. Calendar navigation cannot turn into an endless crawl: dated calendar pages are noindex, navigation links are nofollow and empty far-future months return 404.
  • An easy move from The Events Calendar. A built-in importer copies your events, venues, organizers, categories, ticket types and bookings across without changing anything in The Events Calendar. Event, venue, organizer, month and day URLs follow the same patterns, and an optional setting lets existing [tribe_events] shortcodes keep working, so links and pages survive the switch.
  • Bring your events from anywhere else too. Import from All-in-One Event Calendar, from Eventbrite, from calendar files (.ics) exported by Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar, or from a spreadsheet. Calendar feeds can keep syncing on a schedule.

Calendar and views

  • Six views: month, week, list, photo, map and day, as a block you can place anywhere, plus ready-made templates for block themes. Classic themes are supported too.
  • Search and filters by keyword, category, venue and organizer, applied in place without reloading the page.
  • Mobile friendly. On small screens the month view becomes an easy-to-read agenda.
  • Category colours. Give each category a colour and show it as a line before each event or as the event’s background in the month and week views.
  • Your choice of display. 24-hour or 12-hour times, and full event names in the month view for long titles.
  • Light on your pages. Styles and scripts only load where events are shown, and moving between months and views updates the calendar in place.

Recurring events and time zones

  • Daily, weekly, monthly (“the second Tuesday”, “the last Friday”) and yearly schedules, with intervals, end dates, counts, skipped dates and extra dates (each at the usual time or its own).
  • A custom option for anything else the iCalendar standard can describe.
  • A timezone per event, with correct local times across daylight saving changes.
  • Each date of a repeating event has its own page and its own entry in Google’s event data.

Venues, organizers and maps

  • Create venues and organizers inline while editing an event. Each gets its own page listing its upcoming events.
  • Maps without API keys. OpenStreetMap maps for the calendar, venues and events, with clustered pins, bundled with the plugin.
  • Place venues by typing their coordinates, or turn on address lookup (OpenStreetMap Nominatim, off by default) to find them from the address when you save.

Tickets and RSVP

  • Free RSVP and paid tickets, several ticket types per event, with capacity per type and per date.
  • Stripe Checkout in test and live mode. Connect your Stripe account in one click, or paste a restricted API key.
  • Seats are held while a buyer pays and released automatically if they do not finish, so a date does not oversell.
  • Confirmation emails with ticket codes, an attendee list with check-in, CSV export, one-click refunds and resending confirmations.
  • Your own booking questions on each ticket type (short or long text, dropdown, yes-or-no tick box, phone number), answered once per ticket, with answers on the attendee list, in the CSV and in the emails. Logged-in visitors find their name and email already filled in, which suits membership sites.
  • Reports: bookings, check-ins, no-shows and takings by month, by date and by ticket type for any period, with capacity filled per date and a CSV export for your annual figures.
  • An optional Stripe webhook for instant confirmations. Without it, payments are still confirmed when buyers return and by a background check.
  • Bookings are included in WordPress’s personal data export and erasure tools.

Events sent in by your community

  • A form for your site where people suggest events without a login to wp-admin: name, date and times, description, category, cost, website and an image, a venue and organizer picked from your own lists (or typed in), and their name and email.
  • Every event sent waits as Pending, like a comment awaiting moderation. You are emailed, the Events menu shows how many are waiting, and nothing is public until you publish it. The sender can be emailed when it goes live.
  • Add it with the Submit Event Form block or the [eventward_submit] shortcode. Choose who may send events (anyone, or logged-in people only) under Events > Settings.

Themes, blocks and page builders

  • Native blocks and Site Editor templates for block themes.
  • Shortcodes for the calendar, event details, single fields (date, venue, cost and more), tickets, maps and the event submission form, for Bricks, Divi, Elementor and other builders.
  • A sortable “next date” field for page builder query loops.

Sharing and SEO

  • schema.org Event data on every event: status, attendance mode, location, organizer, price and availability.
  • Add to calendar links for Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, Outlook and Microsoft 365, plus subscribable iCal feeds for the whole calendar or any category.
  • Event status for cancelled, postponed, rescheduled and moved online events, shown on the page and sent to Google.

Fair by default

  • No upsells, no admin banners, no ads and no tracking. Every external service Eventward can use is listed below, with what it sends and when.
  • Your data stays yours: deactivating never deletes anything, and uninstalling only removes events if you ask it to.
  • Translation ready.

Eventward is made by OmnisWP, the team behind Siteward.

External services

Eventward works on your own site, except for the services below:

  • OpenStreetMap Nominatim (geocoding). Off by default: nothing is sent until an admin turns on address lookup under Events > Settings > Maps. When on, it turns venue addresses into map locations. Your site contacts https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org when a venue is saved with a new or changed address, when you press “Find on map”, and in an hourly background check that looks up to 10 venues that have never been looked up (for example imported ones). Venues whose coordinates you typed yourself are never looked up. Each request sends the venue’s address (street, city, region, postcode, country), your site’s address (in the User-Agent, as Nominatim’s policy requires) and your site’s language. Nothing about your visitors is sent. You can turn it off again at any time. Usage policy: https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/nominatim/ Privacy policy: https://osmfoundation.org/wiki/Privacy_Policy
  • OpenStreetMap map tiles. Pages that show a map load map images from https://tile.openstreetmap.org in the visitor’s browser (only once the map scrolls into view). The visitor’s IP address and the page address are visible to that server, as with any image. Tile usage policy: https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/tiles/ Privacy policy: https://osmfoundation.org/wiki/Privacy_Policy You can switch to another tile provider under Events > Settings > Maps.
  • Add to calendar links (Google Calendar, Outlook.com, Microsoft 365) are ordinary links: nothing is sent unless a visitor clicks one.
  • Stripe (payments). Only when you sell paid tickets. Your site talks to https://api.stripe.com to create Stripe Checkout sessions, confirm payments and make refunds. For each checkout your site sends the buyer’s email address, the event title, date and time, the tickets with their prices, an order reference and the addresses of your event page that Stripe returns the buyer to; card details are entered on Stripe’s own page and never touch your site. If you add the optional webhook in your Stripe Dashboard, Stripe also sends payment and refund notices to your site. Stripe terms: https://stripe.com/legal Privacy policy: https://stripe.com/privacy
  • OmnisWP connection service. Only if you choose “Connect with Stripe” instead of pasting an API key. Stripe’s app login needs a secret held by OmnisWP, so https://omniswp.com/wp-json/omnis-connect/v1 is contacted only when an admin presses “Connect with Stripe” (your site first checks the service is available for that mode), and while connected, to renew the short-lived access token: by a background check every 30 minutes, and on demand if the token has run out when your site next talks to Stripe (for example during a booking). When connecting, the admin’s browser takes the mode (test or live), a one-time challenge and the address of your site’s Payments screen to omniswp.com, and your site then sends the one-time claim code and its matching secret to collect the tokens. When renewing, your site sends the mode and the refresh token. Like any WordPress request, these carry your site’s address in the User-Agent. The service never sees payments or buyer details, and keeps nothing after handing the tokens to your site. Terms: https://omniswp.com/terms/ Privacy policy: https://omniswp.com/privacy-policy/
  • Calendar feeds (import, optional). Off until an admin adds a feed under Events > Import > Calendar file or feed. Your site then fetches that address from its own server: once to check it, then on the schedule chosen (hourly, twice a day or daily), and whenever an admin presses Sync now or imports an address with WP-CLI. The requests go only to the addresses you entered (for example Google Calendar or Outlook), identify themselves as Eventward without your site’s address, and carry nothing about your visitors. Delete the feed to stop them. The terms and privacy policy of the calendar service you use apply.
  • Eventbrite (import, optional). Nothing is sent until an admin pastes a private token under Events > Import > Eventbrite and presses Connect. Your site then contacts https://www.eventbriteapi.com to check the token and list the account’s organizations, to count the chosen organization’s events while the Import screen is open, and during an import to read the events, their descriptions, venues, organizers and ticket types. Each request sends the token (in a header), which organization and events to read and, like any WordPress request, your site’s address in the User-Agent. Nothing on Eventbrite is changed and nothing about your visitors is sent. The token is stored encrypted on your site, with the account’s name, email address and organization names, until you press Forget token. Terms: https://www.eventbrite.com/corporate/legal/legalterms/ API terms: https://www.eventbrite.com/help/en-us/articles/833731/eventbrite-api-terms-of-use/ Privacy policy: https://www.eventbrite.com/help/en-us/articles/460838/eventbrite-privacy-policy/
  • Event images during an import. When an import from a calendar file, feed, spreadsheet or Eventbrite includes image addresses and downloading images is ticked (it is by default), your site downloads each image once from the address given (for example Eventbrite’s image server, img.evbuc.com) and adds it to your media library. For feeds this also happens during the scheduled sync. Like any WordPress request, these carry your site’s address in the User-Agent.
